headline: Shinnecock runs blind as buoys go dark, but June thermal math still favors the inlet
subhead: With 44025 offline and the SST package stalled at June 10, the bite call leans on tide mechanics and seasonal water-column structure rather than fresh telemetry.
body_markdown:
The primary offshore reference for this stretch of the South Shore is dark this morning. NOAA buoy 44025, the Long Island station that anchors every honest report from Moriches to Montauk, has its sensor array offline, and 44097 down at Block Island is feeding intermittent water temperature only. The Dr. Fish analyst package itself has no live conditions to publish today, and the satellite SST catalog hasn't refreshed since June 10. That means no clean number to put on the inlet mouth, no shelf-edge gradient to map, and no overnight validation from the field. Reporting around a data gap is part of the job in June, when fog, biofouling, and maintenance windows routinely knock the offshore network down for days at a stretch. What we do know is structural: we are deep into the second week of June, the bay has been warming hard on every flood for two weeks, and the last published SST frames showed the inside water running meaningfully warmer than the ocean side of the inlet.

That inside-outside delta is the engine that matters for this beat right now. Shinnecock Bay in mid-June behaves like a shallow solar collector — Tiana flats, the back side of the barrier beach, and the broad shoals north of the Ponquogue Bridge pick up heat fast, and every outgoing tide flushes that warmer, bait-rich water through the inlet throat into cooler ocean. Bass stack on the ocean side of the jetties and in the rip behind the east jetty tip to ambush whatever the tide hands them: spearing, sand eels, the first real push of bay anchovy, and the small bunker that have been working the bay since late May. Without a buoy number I won't pretend to know the exact thermal break, but the seasonal math says the productive window is the back half of the ebb into the first of the flood, after dark, with the inlet doing the work for you.

The signal from the bay over the past two weeks has been consistent with that pattern. Slot-class bass have been the dominant night-tide class inside the inlet and along the rockpile on the ocean side, with trolled and swum plugs worked low and slow producing better than fast retrieves — a classic sign that the fish are sitting in the current seam rather than chasing through the column. Fluke have set up on the standard early-summer drifts: the channel edges off Ponquogue, the drop into the inlet on the last of the incoming, and the sand-to-grass transitions on the Tiana side. Quality has been better than quantity, with a healthy ratio of keepers to shorts on bucktail-and-Gulp rigs in eight to eighteen feet. Weakfish remain the wildcard at the Ponquogue Bridge pilings on the dusk tide change; the body of fish that showed in late May appears to still be in the system, and the bridge lights at slack-to-outgoing are the highest-percentage shot.

Porgy fishing in the Shinnecock Canal and on the hard bottom up toward the railroad bridge has filled in on schedule, and the canal itself is fishing as the conveyor belt it always is in June — bait moving with every lock cycle, bass and the occasional weakfish staging on the south end. Bluefish presence has been patchy rather than the wall of choppers we sometimes get this week, which tracks with a cooler-than-average ocean side holding them slightly offshore of the beach.

Looking three to five days out, the controlling variable is wind. Any sustained southwest at fifteen-plus will stack warm surface water against the beach and accelerate the inside-outside exchange on the ebb — that is when the inlet jaws get good in a hurry, particularly the two hours before low on the new moon side of this week's lunar cycle. A hard northeast would do the opposite, dropping the bay a couple of degrees and pushing the bass off the structure. I'd be watching the Ponquogue Bridge pilings on the first quiet, humid night after this next frontal passage; that is historically when the weakfish bite goes from a rumor to a pattern. If 44025 comes back online before the weekend, the first reading worth watching is the inlet-mouth surface temperature against the shelf number — anything north of a five-degree spread and the night outgoing becomes the only tide that matters.

Without live buoy data the report is necessarily structural rather than surgical, but the seasonal architecture of this bay is doing exactly what it should be doing in the second week of June, and the fish are responding accordingly. Fish the outgoing, fish it after dark, and let the inlet do the work.
